summary.text: A 46-year-old white male presented with adolescent-onset generalized dystonia, painful posturing of the neck, arms, trunk and toes, and arm tremors that interfered with writing, eating, drinking and dressing. He also had chronic anxiety, depression and panic attacks and an awkward gait without falls. Examination showed neck deviation and tilt, kinetic-predominant mild-moderate arm tremors and no dysmetria; MRI brain and a dystonia gene panel were unremarkable.

Trials of trihexyphenidyl, levodopa-carbidopa, clonazepam, baclofen and repeated botulinum toxin injections brought no improvement, so the symptoms were deemed medication-refractory. He underwent bilateral GPi DBS surgery; the leads were confirmed well placed, the arm tremors responded soon after surgery, and after 6 months of programming the neck dystonia and walking in public spaces improved.

Physical examination at one and 6 months after DBS showed improvement on the Burke Fahn Marsden scale, and SF-36 quality of life improved in many domains. About 2-3 years after surgery he had speech and gait impairment, clear dysmetria in both arms and gait ataxia, which prompted further serum and urine workup. Genetic testing, pursued despite a negative family history, showed an unstable CAG expansion in TBP (22 and 43 repeats), consistent with SCA17.

At 13 years of follow-up the ataxia had progressed, but dystonia and tremor remained improved with DBS on. Accelerometer testing showed a 3 Hz tremor band with a slightly broad half-peak bandwidth, and the tremor peak went away with DBS on. He reported easier activities of daily living and better quality of life than before surgery.

caption_evidence.quote:
FIGURE 2
(A,B) represent accelerometer-based tremor recordings with DBS OFF, and DBS ON DBS (Left GPi, C+ 1-, 3V, 180 PW, 60 Hz; Right GPi, C+ 1-, 3V; 180 PW; 60 Hz), wash-out and wash-in intervals were 30 min respectively. These recordings were performed at the last follow-up visit. The figure illustrates the power spectrum analysis of the tremor signal. The raw signal was digitized, filtered (0–50 Hz) and was subjected to a fast fourier transform (FFT) analysis to generate the frequency peak. We first divided the selected data series (10 s) into overlapping sections of a specified window length, and window overlap and the squared FFT magnitude of each section was averaged and zero-padded to identify the dominant frequency peak. The tremor amplitude was calculated as a square root of the summated power of the frequency peaks recorded along the x, y, and z-axes. The width of the spectral peak at one-half the peak amplitude in the power spectrum was calculated to determine the cycle-to-cycle variability in the frequency (half peak bandwidth > 2 Hz indicates a more irregular tremor).
